ai_summary:
Great Britain’s electricity system is currently operating with a total wind output of 10.8 GW, supported by an estimated Scottish wind output of 3.8 GW, which represents 37.6% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Driven by this high volume of renewable generation, Scottish carbon intensity sits at a clean 0 gCO2/kWh, standing in stark contrast to the GB-wide carbon intensity of 53 gCO2/kWh. 

However, ongoing transmission boundaries prevent this green power from flowing freely to southern demand centers. Consequently, 43.7 GWh of Scottish generation has been curtailed so far today through Balancing Mechanism bids, creating an immediate constraint cost of about £2,772,559. To bridge the resulting deficit, flexible thermal plants have ramped up, requiring an estimated 8,307,389 m3 of gas burned elsewhere and emitting an additional 15,303 tonnes of CO2.

Extrapolating today’s figures across a full year suggests an estimated total yearly cost of curtailment of £1,012 million. When recovered across national network charges over typical annual demand, this financial constraint increases everybody's invoice in the UK by an estimated £3.60/MWh, emphasizing the dual economic and environmental toll of transmission bottlenecks.
